# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

This study compared four coding-agent harnesses with four models on the same ten DeepSWE tasks and measured task success, token use, and normalized cost in 140 canonical trials (@sec-methodology).

## Answer to the research question

The research question asked how different agent harnesses affect the cost efficiency and task-solving performance of coding models on software-engineering tasks. The effect is large, and its direction depends on the model. On the same model and the same tasks, the choice of harness changed the number of solved tasks by up to five of ten and the cost by up to a factor of about two. With Claude Code's delegation on GPT-5.6 Luna, the cost rose by more than an order of magnitude while fewer tasks were solved (@sec-discussion). A harness is therefore not a neutral wrapper around a model but part of what decides how well and how efficiently the model works.

No harness was best on every model. Each harness that led on one model fell behind on another, because features such as delegation, a scripted edit interface, or a shell without a time limit became an advantage or a handicap only through the way a particular model used them. A minimal agent with nothing but a shell reached similar results: on two of the three models with a reference, the best full harness stayed within its range. The additional tools of the full harnesses thus did not reliably solve more tasks.

For cost, the harness decides how many tokens a task consumes and how many of them the provider serves from its cache; the size of the harness's own prompt plays a minor role. Which harness is cheaper also depends on how the model's provider prices cached tokens, so a cost ranking obtained with one model does not transfer to another.

OpenCode V2 was the most consistent harness. It stayed within one task of the best result on all three models it ran on, had the lowest cost per passed task on all three, and kept the highest or nearly the highest cache share, although its native search tools failed in every trial. It did not reach the best result everywhere: on two models, Claude Code solved one task more at a higher cost.

The largest single effect in the study came not from a harness but from the gateway between the harnesses and the models. Defects in the gateway's LiteLLM version withheld the models' earlier reasoning without any error. The affected models then solved less than a third of the tasks they solved otherwise, and about half of the benchmark's billed spend went into runs that the defects made unusable (@sec-discussion-reasoning-loss).

## Recommendations

Three recommendations follow for IONOS SE and for organizations that offer several models to their developers.

First, the harness should be chosen per model where possible. Because no harness was best on every model, agent orchestration interfaces that control several harnesses from one place let users pick the best harness for each model instead of accepting one harness's weaknesses on every model. The results show the practical value of this flexibility.

Second, where one harness is to serve all models, OpenCode V2 is the most consistent choice among the tested harnesses. It needs ripgrep for its search tools and has to keep its `question` tool out of non-interactive runs. It was not tested with Claude models, which dominate current use in the company (@sec-current-state).

Third, evaluations of models, harnesses, and the gateway should be treated as a recurring investment. Small differences in cost or success multiply with every user and every task, whereas an evaluation is paid for once. The gateway defects of this study were found only because the same tasks were measured repeatedly; a small fixed task set, rerun after each change of a model, a harness, or the gateway, would reveal such regressions before they reach users.

## Critical reflection

The results rest on a small sample. Each model--harness combination was run once on ten tasks, so differences of one or two tasks lie within the variation of repeated runs, and the findings describe tendencies rather than statistically confirmed differences (@sec-limitations). Four models were compared, Kimi K3 in only two harnesses, and no Claude model was included for cost reasons. Several conditions had to be repeated after the gateway defects were found, so the canonical trials of some models span several days on a provider whose serving setup is not disclosed. All costs are normalized API prices rather than invoices; where both are available, the billed gateway spend agrees closely with them.

The method developed for this study also shaped the results. The Pier fork, the harness integrations, and the rules for canonical attempts were built for this comparison, and several measurement problems became visible only during the analysis; they are corrected and documented rather than rerun (@sec-measurement-corrections). The prompt-growth check developed to detect the lost reasoning needs only the usage counts of each response and can be reused beyond this study.

## Outlook

Repeated runs on a larger task set would show whether the consistency of OpenCode V2 and the per-model rankings hold beyond single runs. Including Claude models would cover Claude Code in its most common configuration in the company. Running OpenCode V2 with working search tools, and Kimi K3 in OpenCode V2 and Claude Code once the gateway forwards `max` effort, would close the remaining gaps in the benchmark matrix. Finally, the benefit of choosing the harness per model could be measured in daily use, where the same evaluation would also serve as the recurring regression check recommended above.
